processing: A green tea; its specific method is not well recorded. As with other Chinese greens, the leaf is fixed by heat, rolled and dried.
harvest_season: Not documented for this tea; as is usual for Hubei greens, spring picking is the most valued.
appearance_dry: Little is recorded; typical of Hubei named greens, expect neat, dark green leaf.
appearance_liquor: Typical of Hubei green tea, a clear yellow-green.
appearance_wet: Typical of spring green tea: tender, green buds and leaves.
taste_profile: No reliable tasting notes exist for this tea. Expect what is typical of Hubei spring greens: fresh, gently vegetal, with a little sweetness.

brewing.notes: A general starting point for spring green tea.

vintage_note: Usual for its class: sold as the current year's spring harvest and best drunk within the year. It is rarely seen outside Hubei, so details of how it is sold are thin. Ask for the picking date and the producer.
description:
Songzi Bijian is a named green tea from Songzi, in the Jingzhou area of southern Hubei, and it appears on lists of the province's notable greens beside Enshi Yulu and Xianrenzhang. Bijian means something like jade stream.

Very little has been written about how it is made or how it tastes. Assume ordinary green tea work and judge the cup as you would any Hubei spring green, looking for freshness and a clean, gentle sweetness. Keep the water under a boil.

It is a regional tea and hard to find outside the province. If you do run across it, ask who made it and when, since a poetic old name is no guarantee of anything.
history: Hubei's Tang-period teas are said to include one called Bijian Cha, and Songzi Bijian appears among the province's modern named greens. Whether the two are truly continuous is not established, so an ancient lineage should not be assumed. Little else about the tea's development is documented.
